question.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2{e}^{t/2},\,y={e}^{t},\,t\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡3].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
question.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡3.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t/2})={e}^{t/2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{({e}^{t/2})}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{t}+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{t}(1+{e}^{t})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{t/2}\cdot {e}^{t/2}\sqrt{1+{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{t}\sqrt{1+{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{e}^{t}.$ Then, $\text{d}u={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{t}\sqrt{1+{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\pi \cdot {\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}({4}^{3/2}-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}(8-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{3}(4-\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
